CausalChain: Mitochondrial damage -> Enhanced mitophagy -> Excessive degradation of iron-rich mitochondria -> Increased release of mitochondrial iron -> Expansion of the labile iron pool -> Intensified Fenton reaction -> Elevated lipid peroxidation -> Induction of ferroptosis in hepatocytes
Hypothesis: Modulating mitophagy to control the release of mitochondrial iron can regulate hepatic ferroptosis, suggesting that therapeutic strategies targeting mitophagy may protect against ferroptosis-driven liver damage in diseases such as NAFLD and HCC.
Abstract: In this hypothesis, we propose that dysregulated mitophagy in hepatocytes serves as a critical modulator of ferroptosis in liver diseases. Specifically, excessive or imbalanced autophagic clearance of damaged mitochondria may lead to an abnormal release of iron from mitochondrial stores, thereby expanding the labile iron pool. This increase in iron availability can catalyze the Fenton reaction, enhancing lipid peroxidation and ultimately triggering ferroptotic cell death. Such an interplay between mitochondrial quality control and ferroptotic pathways may contribute to the progression of non‐alcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) and hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC). Future investigations into the modulation of mitophagy could uncover novel therapeutic strategies to attenuate ferroptosis-induced liver injury.
